processes.description: Michelle Lokay sends the marketing team a recurring Transwestern summary of average deliveries to California, with utilization and San Juan lateral throughput. Alongside it she circulates capacity postings from the EBB for review before they go up and reminds colleagues that bids close at 5:00 on the due date. Colleagues send supporting files such as contract usage of alternate points or the California interstate capacity report, and questions on contract terms or billing are settled by discussion.
steps: Pull the week's delivery volumes to California and San Juan lateral throughput from the pipeline data.
Work out average deliveries and utilization against capacity.
Send the delivery summary to the marketing team.
Draft a capacity posting and ask colleagues to review it before it is published.
Publish the posting on the EBB and circulate the link.
Remind shippers and colleagues of the bid deadline on the due day.
Gather supporting contract or usage files when a capacity question or billing issue comes up.

stalls.summary: A report went out with the wrong effective date and had to be corrected in a follow-up message.
A capacity posting was published late, and the remark that it happened again suggests a repeated timing problem.

automation.approach: Generate the delivery summary directly from the pipeline's scheduled-volume data: a query fills average deliveries, utilization and lateral throughput into a fixed template, stamps the effective date range automatically, and sends it on a schedule after a quick human check. A posting calendar with automatic bid-deadline reminders would cover the posting and review steps.
automation.rationale: The summary repeats the same sentence with new figures each round, so a fixed report layout fed by the data removes the manual calculation and the date errors seen in the mail. Postings and bids still need judgement, which the reminder calendar supports without replacing.

work_estimate.rationale: Most rounds are the delivery summary: pulling volumes, computing averages and utilization and checking the lateral figure, about 15 to 20 minutes. Rounds that involve a capacity posting, contract file pulls or billing questions take longer. The figure calculation and formatting are routine and largely automatable; review of postings and contract questions are not.

processes.description: Managers and senior staff arrange training for their people: system classes on SAP and the trading systems, a pilot programme, communication and ethics courses, cross-training on the desk and sit-ins with experienced colleagues. A round starts with a request to attend or an announcement of a class; the organiser asks managers to nominate or sign up staff, arranges cover such as night-shift staff arriving early, sets times and meetings, and prepares material or exercises. Approvals are sometimes given in a system that can fail.
steps: A manager, trainer or employee proposes a class, session or sit-in.
The organiser announces the session and asks managers to nominate attendees.
Managers rank or choose staff and send their names to sign up.
Shift cover is arranged so attendees can leave the desk.
The trainer prepares material, exercises or topics for the session.
The enrolment is approved, and the session is held and followed by later units.

stalls.summary: An approver hit a system error when trying to approve a training request, holding up the enrolment.

automation.approach: Keep a shared training calendar with an online sign-up form: managers enter nominees, remaining seats show automatically, approvals route to the right manager, and confirmations and reminders go out without manual messages. A short checklist covers shift cover and preparation of materials.
automation.rationale: The rounds differ in subject but share the same arrangements: nominate, check seats, cover the desk, approve, prepare. A checklist helps the people organising sessions tomorrow; the sign-up form removes the repeated seat and enrolment questions seen in the mail.

work_estimate.rationale: Hands-on work is choosing and ranking attendees, checking seats, arranging shift cover, booking rooms and occasionally preparing exercises or topic lists. Simple sign-ups take a few minutes; rounds where the organiser prepares material or ranks a group take closer to an hour. Scheduling and enrolment are automatable; choosing people and preparing content are not.

processes.description: When a pipeline or supplier cuts scheduled gas, or a meter is shut in, the scheduler reports the cut to the trading and logistics team with the affected supplier, pipeline point and volumes. The desk then finds replacement supply, for example buying gas from another counterparty to resupply, and reschedules. Some rounds come from the counterparty side, such as a customer claiming force majeure or a supplier announcing it will stop deliveries, and need a summary of the affected days.
steps: A pipeline, supplier or field contact reports a cut or shut-in.
The scheduler identifies the affected deals, points, gas days and volumes.
The scheduler sends the cut details to the desk and logistics team.
The trader buys replacement gas or adjusts the sale to cover the shortfall.
Nominations are rescheduled with the pipeline and affected parties are informed.
Force majeure claims or supplier notices are summarised for follow-up.

automation.approach: Feed pipeline cut notices into a standard cut report that looks up the affected deals by point and gas day from the scheduling system, lists the lost volumes, and sends the result to the desk using one message layout. Replacement purchases and rescheduling stay with the trader and scheduler.
automation.rationale: The cut messages carry the same facts each time: supplier, pipeline point, gas day, volume and replacement. A fixed message layout makes them faster to write and read, and a deal lookup removes the manual search; the buying decision still needs a person.

work_estimate.rationale: Each round needs the affected deals and volumes found, replacement gas bought or a sale adjusted, nominations rescheduled and calls made to the pipeline or counterparty. Simple notices take a quarter hour; rounds with resupply purchases or force majeure summaries take longer. Finding affected deals and formatting the notice are automatable; buying and rescheduling decisions are not.
